title: Acute Kidney Injury: Trend the Creatinine, but Watch the Patient
bottomLine: AKI is an abrupt loss of kidney function that can cause fluid overload, hyperkalemia, acidosis, uremia, and medication accumulation. Trend urine output, creatinine, potassium, volume status, and nephrotoxin exposure; immediately escalate severe hyperkalemia, pulmonary edema, progressive oliguria/anuria, or uremic complications.
recognize: Rising creatinine and/or reduced urine output
Prerenal clues: volume loss, hypotension, poor perfusion
Intrinsic clues: nephrotoxins, glomerular/interstitial disease, prolonged ischemia
Postrenal clues: obstruction, retention, enlarged prostate, stones, pelvic mass
assess: Strict intake/output, daily weight, edema, lung sounds, BP/perfusion
Trend creatinine/BUN, potassium, bicarbonate, sodium, phosphate and other ordered labs
Review medications/contrast exposure and check for bladder distention/obstruction
actions: Treat the cause according to orders: restore perfusion, stop/adjust nephrotoxins through prescriber/pharmacy, relieve obstruction, manage fluids/electrolytes
Avoid automatic fluid boluses when the patient is already overloaded
Prepare for renal replacement therapy when ordered for refractory life-threatening complications
diagnostics: Urinalysis, urine microscopy, ultrasound and selected serologies help define cause
Creatinine lags behind acute injury; urine-output trend and clinical context matter
medicationSafety: Renally cleared drugs can accumulate during AKI
NSAIDs, contrast and other nephrotoxins require risk review
ACE inhibitor/ARB, diuretics and other medications may need temporary adjustment based on cause/hemodynamics—follow the authorized plan
teaching: Avoid nonprescribed NSAID overuse and dehydration, and follow medication/lab instructions after AKI
Report reduced urine output, swelling, dyspnea, or recurrent vomiting
scopeAndDelegation: PN/LVN priorities are accurate fluid balance, trend recognition, safe medication administration, and escalation. Medication-dose adjustment and dialysis initiation are clinician/team decisions.
examTrap: Giving large volumes of fluid solely because urine output is low without assessing whether the patient is hypovolemic, obstructed, or already fluid overloaded.
oneLinePearl: AKI: cause + potassium + fluid + drug accumulation.

title: Chronic Kidney Disease: Fluid, Potassium, Anemia, Bone, and Medications
bottomLine: CKD affects more than creatinine: monitor volume/BP, potassium/acidosis, anemia, mineral-bone disease, nutrition, medication clearance, cardiovascular risk, and progression. Sudden worsening from baseline is AKI-on-CKD until evaluated, not automatically 'expected renal disease.'
recognize: Fatigue, pruritus, edema, hypertension, nocturia early/oliguria late, nausea, cognitive changes in advanced disease
Anemia from reduced erythropoietin/iron issues
Hyperphosphatemia, low/altered calcium and secondary hyperparathyroidism contribute to bone disease
assess: Weight/edema, BP, lung sounds, intake/output, vascular access if dialysis
Trend eGFR/creatinine, potassium, bicarbonate, hemoglobin/iron, calcium/phosphate/PTH as ordered
Review OTC/herbal products and renal-dose medications
actions: Administer ordered antihypertensive/renal protective therapy and monitor response
Follow individualized sodium, potassium, phosphate, protein and fluid guidance
Provide anemia/mineral-bone therapies as ordered
Protect future dialysis access sites when appropriate
diagnostics: eGFR and urine albumin quantify CKD severity/risk
A sudden creatinine change is not staged as chronic progression without context
medicationSafety: Many antibiotics, anticoagulants, diabetes drugs, gabapentinoids, opioids and others require renal-dose review
Magnesium/aluminum-containing OTC products can accumulate in advanced CKD
NSAIDs can worsen kidney function and fluid/BP control
teaching: Medication reconciliation including OTCs, BP/diabetes management, kidney-protective follow-up, dietitian plan, and when to report fluid/electrolyte symptoms
scopeAndDelegation: The PN/LVN reinforces the individualized renal plan and monitors complications. Diet, medication dose, dialysis timing and transplant decisions are made by the nephrology/team plan.
examTrap: Assuming a standard 'renal diet' is identical for every CKD patient regardless of potassium, phosphate, dialysis status, nutrition, and comorbidity.
oneLinePearl: CKD is a whole-body disease: fluid, electrolytes, blood, bone, heart, drugs.

title: Hyperkalemia: Stabilize the Heart, Shift Potassium, Remove Potassium
bottomLine: Severe hyperkalemia can kill through dysrhythmia. Verify a suspicious nonhemolyzed result when appropriate, put severe/symptomatic patients on cardiac monitoring, give IV calcium for membrane stabilization when indicated, shift potassium intracellularly with ordered insulin/dextrose and beta-agonist therapy, and remove potassium through diuresis/binders/dialysis as appropriate.
recognize: Weakness, paresthesias, nausea may occur but patients can be asymptomatic
ECG may progress through peaked T waves, PR/QRS changes, bradyarrhythmia or sine-wave patterns; absence of ECG change does not prove safety
Causes: kidney failure, tissue breakdown, acidosis, insulin deficiency, RAAS drugs, potassium-sparing diuretics, supplements
assess: Potassium value/trend and specimen hemolysis
Continuous rhythm, HR/BP/perfusion for severe cases
Renal function, glucose, acid-base status, medication/supplement list
Recheck potassium and glucose after treatment
actions: Escalate severe hyperkalemia or ECG change immediately
Administer IV calcium as ordered to stabilize myocardium
Give insulin with dextrose and/or nebulized beta-agonist per protocol
Administer potassium-removal therapy and prepare for dialysis when refractory/severe with renal failure
diagnostics: Repeat potassium when pseudohyperkalemia is plausible but do not delay treatment of a critically high value with ECG instability
ECG is essential but not sensitive enough to rule out risk
medicationSafety: Insulin can cause delayed hypoglycemia—monitor glucose for the protocol-defined period
IV calcium does not lower serum potassium; it buys cardiac protection time
Stop potassium-containing products and clarify contributing medications through the care team
teaching: Follow individualized potassium/medication guidance; salt substitutes may contain potassium
Do not stop beneficial RAAS medications independently—hyperkalemia management requires clinician review
scopeAndDelegation: The PN/LVN recognizes critical potassium/ECG changes, gives ordered emergency therapy within competency, monitors glucose/rhythm, and escalates. IV calcium/insulin protocols may be higher-acuity policy restricted.
examTrap: Giving sodium polystyrene or another binder as the only first treatment for a patient with severe hyperkalemia and dangerous ECG changes.
oneLinePearl: HyperK: calcium protects heart, insulin shifts K, removal fixes body burden.

title: Hemodialysis: Protect the Access and Expect Hemodynamic Shifts
bottomLine: A functioning AV fistula/graft should have a thrill/bruit; loss of either is urgent. Protect the access from BP cuffs, venipuncture, compression and infection. Around dialysis, watch for hypotension, cramping, dysrhythmia/electrolyte shifts, bleeding and access complications.
recognize: Thrill palpated and bruit auscultated over AV access
Access infection: redness, warmth, drainage, fever
Steal/ischemia: cool painful hand, reduced perfusion
Dialysis disequilibrium is a neurologic complication during/after rapid solute shifts, especially early treatments
assess: Pre/post weight, BP, edema/lung sounds, symptoms
Access thrill/bruit, skin, bleeding, distal perfusion
Review labs and medication timing around dialysis per plan
actions: Protect access limb
For post-dialysis bleeding, use direct pressure without occluding the entire access and escalate persistent bleeding
Assist with hypotension management according to dialysis protocol
Report absent thrill/bruit immediately
diagnostics: Dialysis adequacy and labs guide the dialysis prescription; the bedside nurse focuses on clinical response and access status
medicationSafety: Some antihypertensives and dialyzable medications have specific timing instructions—follow the nephrology plan
Heparin used during dialysis increases bleeding risk
Do not administer medications through an AV fistula/graft unless specifically authorized for dialysis access use
teaching: Daily access check, hygiene, no tight clothing/jewelry/compression, avoid sleeping on access arm, report absent thrill or infection
scopeAndDelegation: Dialysis procedures and access cannulation require dialysis-specific competency. A PN/LVN outside that role protects and assesses the access and reports complications; do not use it like a routine IV.
examTrap: Taking a BP or drawing blood from the fistula arm because the other arm has an IV.

title: Peritoneal Dialysis: Cloudy Effluent Is Peritonitis Until Evaluated
bottomLine: Peritoneal dialysis depends on sterile connection technique and free inflow/outflow. Cloudy effluent, abdominal pain, fever, nausea or systemic illness raises concern for PD peritonitis; obtain the ordered effluent specimen and start directed therapy promptly. Poor drainage requires mechanical assessment before assuming membrane failure.
recognize: Expected effluent is generally clear; fibrin may occur without infection but cloudy fluid is concerning
Peritonitis: abdominal pain/tenderness, cloudy effluent, fever or malaise
Poor outflow: constipation, kinks, position, catheter migration, fibrin or obstruction
assess: Effluent clarity/color/amount, inflow/outflow time, abdominal symptoms, temperature
Exit site/tunnel for redness/drainage
Daily weight, BP, edema, glucose in diabetic patients
actions: Use meticulous aseptic/sterile connection technique per PD system
If cloudy effluent, notify promptly and collect specimen before antibiotics when ordered without delaying needed therapy
Reposition/check tubing/constipation plan for poor flow
Warm dialysate only with approved equipment—never microwave
diagnostics: Effluent cell count/differential and culture diagnose peritonitis
Do not discard cloudy effluent before the specimen can be obtained if ordered
medicationSafety: Intraperitoneal antibiotics are often used for PD peritonitis under nephrology protocol
Dialysate contains glucose and can raise blood glucose
Adding medications to dialysate requires exact sterile pharmacy/nephrology instructions
redFlags: No outflow with worsening respiratory/abdominal symptoms
teaching: Hand hygiene/mask and connection technique, exit-site care, daily effluent inspection, constipation prevention, and immediate reporting of cloudy fluid
scopeAndDelegation: PN/LVN PD roles depend on home/facility dialysis competency. Never improvise dialysate additives or catheter manipulation outside protocol.
examTrap: Continuing exchanges and throwing away cloudy drainage without notifying the team or obtaining the ordered culture specimen.
oneLinePearl: PD: clear in, clear out; cloudy out needs action.
sourceBasis: International Society for Peritoneal Dialysis peritonitis guidance

title: UTI vs Pyelonephritis: When a Bladder Infection Moves Upstream
bottomLine: Lower UTI usually causes dysuria, frequency and urgency; fever, flank pain/CVA tenderness, vomiting or systemic illness suggests pyelonephritis or complicated infection. Older adults still need symptom-based assessment—bacteriuria alone does not prove a UTI caused nonspecific confusion.
recognize: Cystitis: dysuria, frequency, urgency, suprapubic discomfort
Pyelonephritis: fever/chills, flank pain/CVA tenderness, nausea/vomiting, systemic symptoms
Pregnancy, obstruction, catheter, male anatomy, immunocompromise or renal disease can complicate infection
assess: Vitals, hydration, pain, urinary symptoms, flank/CVA findings, pregnancy possibility
Assess sepsis signs and ability to keep fluids/medications down
Review catheter necessity and recent antibiotics/cultures
actions: Collect urine correctly before antibiotics when ordered and feasible
Administer prescribed antimicrobial/analgesic therapy and fluids as appropriate
Escalate sepsis, obstruction, pregnancy-related pyelonephritis or inability to tolerate oral therapy
diagnostics: Urinalysis supports inflammation; urine culture identifies organism/susceptibility when indicated
Asymptomatic bacteriuria is not treated in most populations except specific indications such as pregnancy or certain urologic procedures
medicationSafety: Renal function, allergies, pregnancy and culture susceptibility affect antibiotic choice
Phenazopyridine relieves urinary discomfort but does not treat infection and can discolor urine
teaching: Complete antibiotics, hydrate as appropriate, void regularly, and seek care for fever/flank pain/worsening symptoms
scopeAndDelegation: PN/LVN collects accurate specimens, gives ordered treatment, monitors response and sepsis signs, and avoids labeling nonspecific symptoms as UTI without clinical evidence.
examTrap: Treating a positive urine culture in an otherwise asymptomatic older adult as the automatic cause of confusion.
oneLinePearl: Flank + fever = think upper tract; bacteria alone is not a diagnosis.

title: Kidney Stones: Pain Is Expected; Infection Plus Obstruction Is Not
bottomLine: Renal colic can cause severe waxing/waning flank pain, hematuria and nausea. The dangerous combination is an obstructed urinary system plus infection—fever, systemic illness or pyuria with obstruction requires urgent urologic drainage rather than pain medicine alone.
recognize: Acute flank pain radiating toward groin, restlessness, hematuria, nausea
Fever/rigors are not routine uncomplicated stone symptoms
Solitary kidney, pregnancy, renal failure or anuria raises urgency
assess: Vitals, pain, urine output, hydration, fever/sepsis signs
Strain urine if ordered for stone analysis
Assess pregnancy possibility and prior stones
actions: Give ordered analgesia/antiemetic and hydration plan
Encourage mobility/fluids only as appropriate—not forced excessive fluid during complete obstruction
Urgently escalate infection with obstruction, anuria, uncontrolled pain or AKI
diagnostics: Noncontrast CT is common in adults; ultrasound is used in selected patients including pregnancy
Urinalysis/culture evaluate blood/infection; renal function assesses obstruction impact
medicationSafety: NSAIDs are effective renal-colic analgesics for many patients but require renal/GI/bleeding risk review
Alpha blockers may be used selectively to assist passage; monitor hypotension
teaching: Capture stone if instructed, maintain individualized hydration, and follow stone-analysis dietary prevention rather than generic restriction
Seek urgent care for fever or inability to urinate
scopeAndDelegation: PN/LVN manages ordered symptom care, tracks urine/output, strains urine when ordered, and recognizes infected obstruction. Imaging/procedural selection is clinician/urology directed.
examTrap: Reassuring a stone patient with fever because severe pain and hematuria are 'normal for stones.'
sourceBasis: American Urological Association kidney stone guidance

title: Acute Urinary Retention: Full Bladder, Empty Problem List? No.
bottomLine: Acute urinary retention causes suprapubic fullness/pain, inability to void or overflow dribbling and can lead to AKI/infection. Confirm bladder volume when appropriate, identify reversible causes, decompress with ordered catheterization when indicated, and monitor urine output/hemodynamics after relief of large/chronic obstruction.
recognize: Unable to void, frequent small amounts/overflow, suprapubic distention/discomfort
Causes: BPH/obstruction, postoperative anesthesia, anticholinergics/opioids, neurogenic bladder, constipation
Older or neurologically impaired patients may show agitation rather than report pain
assess: Last void, intake/output, bladder palpation/scan, pain
Review medications, recent surgery/anesthesia, bowel status, neuro symptoms
After decompression, monitor output and blood pressure if high-volume retention
actions: Use bladder scan when available/appropriate before unnecessary catheterization
Perform ordered intermittent/indwelling catheterization using sterile technique
Treat constipation/medication/obstruction cause through the care plan
Report post-obstructive polyuria or hematuria
diagnostics: Post-void residual quantifies retention
Urinalysis/renal tests/imaging depend on cause and complications
medicationSafety: Anticholinergics, opioids and some antihistamines can worsen retention
Alpha blockers can cause orthostatic hypotension
teaching: Medication review, timed voiding/catheter plan when indicated, constipation prevention, and return precautions for inability to void
scopeAndDelegation: Catheterization is commonly PN/LVN practice with competency, but retention assessment/management follows state/facility policy. New neuro deficits require urgent escalation, not routine catheter care only.
examTrap: Treating new retention with catheterization alone while ignoring saddle numbness/leg weakness suggesting spinal compression.
oneLinePearl: Retention: scan, drain when ordered, then ask why.

title: Urinary Catheters: The Best CAUTI Prevention Is Not Needing One
bottomLine: Use an indwelling urinary catheter only for an appropriate indication and remove it as soon as it is no longer needed. Insert aseptically, keep a closed dependent drainage system with unobstructed flow, keep the bag below bladder level, and obtain cultures from the sampling port—not the bag.
recognize: Risk rises with catheter duration and breaks in the closed system
Cloudy/odorous urine alone does not diagnose CAUTI
Catheter obstruction/kinking can cause retention and bladder injury
assess: Daily indication, urine output/character, tubing position, bag location, meatal/skin condition
Assess fever/systemic or urinary symptoms before labeling CAUTI
Check for alternatives such as intermittent catheterization/external devices when appropriate
actions: Use sterile insertion technique and secure catheter
Maintain closed system and unobstructed drainage
Perform routine perineal hygiene—not antiseptic irrigation
Remove promptly when indication ends
diagnostics: For culture, obtain fresh urine aseptically from the sampling port after appropriate preparation; do not culture from the drainage bag
medicationSafety: Do not use prophylactic antibiotics routinely solely because a catheter is present unless a specific indication exists
teaching: Keep drainage bag below bladder and off floor; avoid pulling/disconnecting tubing; report fever/pain or no drainage
scopeAndDelegation: PN/LVN may insert/manage catheters with competency. Daily necessity assessment should prompt removal/clarification through the authorized plan; assistive staff can perform hygiene but must report obstruction/leakage/output changes.
examTrap: Disconnecting the catheter to obtain a sterile specimen or raising the drainage bag onto the bed for convenience.
oneLinePearl: CAUTI prevention: indication, aseptic insertion, closed flow, early removal.

title: Nephrotic Syndrome: Protein Loss, Edema, Clot and Infection Risk
bottomLine: Nephrotic syndrome causes heavy protein loss leading to hypoalbuminemia, edema and hyperlipidemia, with increased thrombosis and infection risk. Track weight/edema, skin, respiratory status, urine protein, kidney function and thrombotic symptoms; treat the cause and complications according to the renal plan.
recognize: Generalized/periorbital edema, foamy urine, weight gain
Heavy proteinuria/hypoalbuminemia
VTE risk and infection susceptibility
assess: Daily weight, edema, BP, skin integrity, lung sounds
Urine protein and renal labs as ordered
Assess new unilateral swelling, chest pain/dyspnea, fever/infection
actions: Follow sodium/fluid plan and prescribed diuretics
Skin protection and mobility/VTE prevention
Administer disease-specific immunosuppression/ACEi/ARB/anticoagulation only as ordered
diagnostics: Urine protein quantification and serum albumin/lipids support syndrome
Biopsy/serologies identify cause when needed
medicationSafety: Diuretics can cause intravascular depletion/electrolyte shifts despite edema
Immunosuppression increases infection risk
Anticoagulation decisions balance thrombotic and bleeding risk
teaching: Daily weights, infection/VTE warning signs, medication adherence and individualized sodium/protein guidance
scopeAndDelegation: PN/LVN monitors edema/weight/skin and complications; renal cause and immunosuppressive/anticoagulation strategy are clinician decisions.
examTrap: Assuming edema always means the intravascular space is overloaded and giving unmonitored aggressive diuresis despite hypotension.
oneLinePearl: Nephrotic = protein out, edema up, clot/infection risk up.

title: Acute Glomerulonephritis: Hematuria, Hypertension, and Fluid Retention
bottomLine: Nephritic/glomerulonephritic syndromes commonly present with hematuria, proteinuria, hypertension, edema and reduced kidney function. The bedside danger is fluid overload, severe hypertension, hyperkalemia or AKI; trend weight, BP, urine and renal/electrolyte function while the cause is evaluated.
recognize: Tea/cola-colored urine or microscopic hematuria
Periorbital edema, hypertension, reduced urine
May follow infection or reflect autoimmune/rapidly progressive kidney disease
assess: BP, weight/edema, lung sounds, urine output/appearance
Creatinine, potassium, urinalysis/protein and immune/infectious studies as ordered
Assess systemic rash/joint/lung symptoms for broader disease
actions: Follow fluid/sodium restriction and antihypertensive/diuretic plan
Treat underlying infection/immune disease only as ordered
Escalate rapidly worsening renal function, pulmonary edema or severe BP
diagnostics: Urinalysis may show blood/protein/casts
Complement, antibodies, infection tests and kidney biopsy identify cause in selected cases
medicationSafety: Renal impairment changes drug clearance
Immunosuppressive treatment carries infection risk
Avoid nephrotoxins unless benefit outweighs risk and ordered
redFlags: Hemoptysis plus renal failure suggesting pulmonary-renal syndrome
teaching: Monitor BP/weight and report declining urine, dyspnea or severe headache
Complete follow-up even if urine color improves
scopeAndDelegation: PN/LVN trends renal/hemodynamic status and supports ordered treatment; diagnostic classification/biopsy/immunosuppression decisions are nephrology-directed.
examTrap: Focusing on the dramatic urine color while missing severe hypertension and pulmonary fluid overload.
oneLinePearl: Nephritic pattern: blood + pressure + fluid + falling filtration.

title: Rhabdomyolysis: Muscle Breakdown Can Become Kidney and Potassium Failure
bottomLine: Rhabdomyolysis releases myoglobin and intracellular electrolytes after major muscle injury, prolonged immobilization, seizures, exertional heat illness, toxins/drugs and other causes. The major bedside threats are hyperkalemia, AKI, hypovolemia and compartment syndrome; start ordered fluids promptly when appropriate and trend urine, potassium, creatinine and CK.
recognize: Muscle pain/weakness/swelling; dark urine may occur but the classic triad is not always present
Risks: crush injury, prolonged down time, seizures, hyperthermia, extreme exertion, drugs/toxins
Hyperkalemia can cause lethal dysrhythmia before creatinine rises
assess: Vitals/perfusion, urine output/color, muscle swelling/pain, neurovascular status
CK, potassium, creatinine, calcium/phosphate, urinalysis as ordered
Continuous ECG for significant hyperkalemia
actions: Give ordered isotonic fluids while watching for overload
Treat hyperkalemia immediately when severe
Stop/clarify offending medications through prescriber and treat cause
Assess for compartment syndrome
diagnostics: Marked CK elevation supports diagnosis; urine heme may be positive with few RBCs when myoglobin present
Do not wait for dark urine to suspect rhabdomyolysis
medicationSafety: Statins can rarely cause serious myopathy/rhabdomyolysis, especially with interacting drugs
Potassium-containing fluids/supplements require review if hyperkalemia is present
redFlags: Severe limb swelling with pain/passive stretch or neurovascular compromise
teaching: Report severe unexplained muscle pain/weakness or dark urine after medication changes or intense exertion; maintain appropriate hydration during heat/exertion
scopeAndDelegation: PN/LVN monitors fluids/urine/electrolyte warning signs and administers ordered treatment. Aggressive fluid targets and dialysis decisions are clinician-directed.
examTrap: Waiting for kidney failure before treating severe hyperkalemia in a patient with major muscle breakdown.
oneLinePearl: Rhabdo threatens kidneys, potassium, and compartments.
